How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Offspring survival depends on parental behavior, both for providing immediate protection from danger, and for transmitting information about what is dangerous and how best to avoid it. In rodents, the presence of offspring changes parental responses to danger, facilitating active threat coping over freezing. We investigated whether offspring presence reshapes human parental defense in a similar way, and whether parental defense in turn affects how effectively children learn vicariously about threats. We developed a virtual reality-based naturalistic paradigm where parents were able to display unconstrained defensive responses to a virtual attacker. Eighty-five parents participated with their own child, and forty with an unrelated child.

All parents performed the task twice, once alone and once in the presence of the own/unrelated child. With their own child relative to alone, parents showed reduced freezing-like behavior, fought the attacker faster and more precisely, and stayed closer to their child. In turn, children sharing the environment with their parent showed enhanced physiological differentiation of sound cues predicting threat or safety. Moreover, increased proximity to the parent (but not to an unrelated adult) enhanced attack expectancy reported by the child afterwards. Altogether, our findings parallel and extend prior reports in rodents, and suggest that offspring presence induces an evolutionarily conserved reorganization of parental defense that facilitates both offspring protection and transmission of threat information.

Main

When confronted with danger, animals must select among alternative defensive strategies.

Strategies that maximize personal safety may leave vulnerable offspring unprotected, whereas effective offspring protection may require confronting threats despite risks to oneself. Rodent studies suggest that offspring presence reorganizes defensive behavior in parents, for instance by suppressing freezing and promoting active threat coping strategies 1 . Whether offspring presence similarly affects defensive behavior in human parents remains unknown. Addressing this question is important not only for understanding parental adaptations in humans but also because parental responses to threat may shape how children learn about danger. We developed an interactive experimental task to examine whether and how human parental defense is reconfigured by the presence of offspring, and whether variation in defensive responding influences observational threat learning in children.

Evidence from rodent models suggests that parenthood may reconfigure defense in ways that facilitate offspring protection. During pregnancy and lactation, females exhibit a range of behavioral adaptations that promote offspring survival, including increased caregiving behaviors (e.g., nursing, retrieval) and defensive aggression towards intruders. The increased maternal aggression has been linked to coordinated neuroendocrine changes involving the oxytocinarginine vasopressin (OXT/AVP) and corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) systems 2, 3 . Recent findings also suggest that hormones prolactin and oxytocin during lactation may activate specific hypothalamic neurons otherwise dormant in females, and contribute directly to aggressive behaviors 4 . These changes extend beyond aggression. Indeed, lactating dams have been proposed to be less "fearful" in general, showing reduced freezing in the presence of pups 1, 5 , increased exploratory behavior 6 , and less defensive burying 7 . Rather than reflecting an overall reduction of defensive responding, these observations point to a reconfiguration of defensive strategies that favors offspring protection over self-defense 8 . Similar to rodents, parenthood in humans is accompanied by profound hormonal, neural and motivational changes in both mothers [9] [10] [11] and fathers 12, 13 . These changes have primarily been described in the initial transition to parenthood, with most studies focusing on how they relate to responsiveness to infant-related cues 14 and support bonding and parental investment 15, 16.

Whether parenthood also recalibrates defensive priorities toward offspring protection remains unclear. Changes in parental defensive behaviors, and their consequences for children, are under-researched in humans. There are reports that breastfeeding 17 and oxytocin administration 18 may promote maternal protective behaviors, but results have not been consistently replicated. Importantly, it is unknown how offspring presence reshapes parental defensive behavior.

Findings from rodent work offer key mechanistic insights into the defensive adaptations that support parental care. Translating those findings into human experimental models may thus help to develop a mechanistic and neurobiologically grounded account of how parenthood shapes defense. Such approach is particularly valuable when combined with ecologically valid paradigms that account for fundamental interspecies differences between rodents and humans.

To test whether offspring presence reorganizes defensive strategy selection in human parents, we developed a naturalistic virtual reality (VR) paradigm (Figure 1a) designed to elicit unconstrained defensive behaviors. Two samples participated in the study, one including biological parent-child dyads (own-child sample) and a control sample including parentunrelated child dyads (unrelated-child sample). Parents navigated an immersive virtual environment depicting a forest at night and were informed of the potential presence of a virtual attacker (Figure 1b). In each trial, the defensive context dynamically changed based on the predatory imminence continuum 19 : initially, no attacker was present (pre-encounter); subsequently, the attacker could be seen wandering in the distance (post-encounter); finally, in half of the trials, an attack would actually be initiated (circa-strike) and could result in the administration of an aversive electrical shock to the parent's wrist. This framework allowed parents to express a range of context-dependent defensive responses (e.g., if the attacker was far, reduced movement could prevent detection; if an attack was ongoing, fighting back would lower the probability of shock; Figure 1). Defensive behavior was quantified via behavioral, kinematic, and physiological indices. To determine whether defense was modulated by offspring presence, parents from both samples performed the task alone and in the presence of the own/unrelated child in counterbalanced order (henceforth, referred to as alone and with-child conditions, respectively). When present, the child passively shared the virtual environment with the parent/unrelated adult; they were not required to perform any behavior and were not at risk of receiving shocks, but could see (and be seen by) the parent/unrelated adult.

Rodent work suggests that offspring presence suppresses parental freezing and shifts defensive behavior towards more active strategies that either target the threat or facilitate contact with the pups 1 . We therefore hypothesized that, in the presence of their child, human parents would exhibit reduced passive responses (e.g., freezing) and increased active defense, including greater movement and more vigorous attempts to confront the threat. Observed effects of child presence on parental defense were also tested in the unrelated-child sample to determine whether they reflected a parenthood-related adaptation or a general social modulation effect not specific to kin.

Defensive behavior serves not only to manage immediate danger but also provides observable information about threat value. Consequently, any offspring-driven reorganization of parental defense may have downstream consequences for how children learn about environmental threats. Indeed, rodent research shows that the type of threat-coping behavior expressed by progenitors affects social threat learning in offspring. Rickenbacher and colleagues 1 reported that only pups whose mothers did not freeze to a conditioned threat were later shown to freeze to the same stimulus. There is evidence that human children acquire threat information through observational learning of parents 20 , with stronger learning from observing parents relative to unrelated adults 21 , and increased physiological synchrony between parent and child promoting observational learning 22 , particularly in children with insecure attachment 23 . However, such findings were obtained in traditional observational learning procedures, in which the behavior of the parent is highly constrained by the task 24 . Thus, it is unknown whether the type of defensive behavior displayed by parents (e.g., whether they predominantly freeze or fight) affects the effectiveness of threat learning in children. A second goal of our study was therefore to determine how observational threat learning in human children is impacted by parental defensive behavior.

To investigate this question, we embedded an observational learning component within the VR paradigm (Figure 1b). In half of the trials, the virtual attacker attacked the parent (the attack constituting the unconditioned stimulus, US), whereas in the remaining trials no attack occurred.

Before each trial, participants heard one of two environmental sounds, an owl or a frog, that served as conditioned stimuli, CS. Across participants, either sound served as the CS+, consistently predicting attack trials, whereas the other served as the CS-, consistently predicting no-attack trials. Observational learning in children was assessed in two ways. First, during the with-child condition, which served as an acquisition phase for the child, we measured their differential skin conductance response to CS+ and CS-sounds. Second, we introduced a subsequent test phase, in which the child remained alone in the virtual environment; here, CS+ and CS-sounds were replayed, and the child was asked to rate how likely it was that each sound was followed by an attack on the parent in the previous block. Based on rodent findings suggesting that offspring preferentially acquire threat information when mothers suppress freezing responses 1 , we hypothesized that greater active defense by parents in the presence of the child would predict stronger observational threat learning in children.

In sum, we expected that the presence of children would trigger enhanced active defense from parents (relative to alone), and that active parental defense would in turn predict stronger threat learning in children. and no attack would take place; 7s). To fight back during circa-strike, participants were instructed to approach the attacker and repeatedly press a button on a joystick, which in the VR environment corresponded to hitting him with a stick. Participants performed the task in two counterbalanced conditions (alone and with-child). The with-child condition included two dyad types: own-child and unrelated-child. In the with-child condition, the child (either the participant's own child or an unrelated child) was represented as an avatar standing by the tent and were able to see the (own or unrelated) parent's avatar perform the task. An observational conditioning procedure was embedded in the with-child condition. Two environmental sounds (an owl and a frog) served as conditioned stimuli, CS. Across participants, one sound was designated the CS+ and consistently predicted attack trials, whereas the other served as the CS-and consistently predicted no-attack trials. Sounds were presented three times per trial, with 0-1 s jitter added to reduce onset predictability: at the beginning of the post-encounter phase, immediately before attack onset (circa-strike), and midway through the attack phase (or the corresponding time point in no-attack trials).

Results

Parents under threat prioritize proximity to own children

We first assessed how the presence of offspring influenced the target of human parental defense, i.e., whether parents under threat predominantly displayed threat-directed or childdirected behaviors. One approach taken to determine this was to compare how close, and for how long, parents stayed in the center of the environment when they were alone versus in the presence of their child. Given that, when present, the child held a stationary position close to the center of the environment, increased proximity to the center also results in increased proximity to the child. Results of a linear mixed model showed that, across phases of threat imminence (pre-encounter, post-encounter and circa-strike), average distance from the center was shorter when the child was present (β(with-child)=-0.08, SE=0.02, t=-4.85, p<0.001; Table S2). A significant phase by condition interaction (β(with-child: post-encounter)=-0.01, SE=0.005, t=-2.97, p=0.004; β(with-child: circa-strike)=-0.02, SE=0.01, t=3.27, p=0.002), followed up on by examination of the estimated marginal means (Table S3), suggested this effect was especially pronounced during pre-and post-encounter, although also present in circa-strike (Figure 2a).

Similarly, longer time in the center was registered across phases when the child was present (β(with-child)=0.08, SE=0.02, t=3.62, p<0.001; Table S11) with a reduced effect in the circa-strike phase (β(with-child: circa-strike)=0.03, SE=0.01, t=-2.36, p=0.021; Figure 2b), although the effect remained significant in all three phases (all ps<0.01; Table S8). That parents stayed closer to, and for longer in the center when their child was present suggests maintaining proximity to offspring is prioritized during human parental defense, and that this tendency is reduced when an attack becomes imminent.

To rule out the possibility that these effects reflect a general social modulation of defensive behavior, i.e., are driven by the presence of another individual regardless of kinship, the same models were fit to the unrelated-child sample (N=38 dyads; age-and sex-matched to the ownchild sample; Table S1). Similar to the first experiment, each parent was tested alone and in the presence of an unrelated child. When modelling the distance from the center from both samples together (using sample as an additional between-subjects fixed-effect), we did not find any significant three-way interaction between condition, phase and sample (β(with-child: postencounter: unrelated-child)=0.02, SE=0.01, t=1.60, p=0.111; β(with-child: circa-strike: unrelated-child)=0.005, SE=0.01, t=0.35, p=0.730; Table S6), However, follow-up comparisons showed that child presence had an effect on the distance from the center in all phases for the own-child sample, but only in pre-encounter for the unrelated-child (p=0.044; Table S8). Also, a follow-up model on the unrelated-child sample revealed that, contrary to the own-child sample, the distance of the parent to the center did not differ significantly when they were alone versus with an unrelated child (β(unrelated-child)=-0.05, SE=0.04, t=-1.34, p=0.189; Table S4). Even though we observed a significant condition by phase interaction (β(with-child: circa-strike)=-0.03, SE=0.01, t=2.23, p=0.032), follow up comparisons did not reveal any significant withinphase differences in the distance from the center when they were alone compared to with the child (all ps>0.1; Figure 2a; Table S5). Altogether, these results suggest that the effect of child presence on parental distance from the center were at least partly kin-specific.

For the time spent in the center, the full model revealed that parents in the unrelated-child sample spent significantly less time in the center than those in the own-child sample (β(unrelated-child)=-0.08, SE=0.03, t=-2.47, p=0.015; Table S16). Notably, there were interactions between sample and condition (β(with-child: unrelated-child)=-0.10, SE=0.05, t=-1.93, p=0.056), and sample and phase (β(post-encounter: unrelated-child)=0.029, SE=0.01, t=-2.58, p=0.011). Follow-up analyses revealed that, during pre-and post-encounter, differences between alone and with-child conditions were only observed in the own-child sample (both ps=0.032; Figure 2b; Table S18), with parents spending more time in the center only when accompanied by their own child. Taken together, our findings suggest that parents under threat selectively prioritize proximity to their own child, providing evidence for a kin-specific modulation of defensive behavior.

Reduced parental freezing in the presence of own children

One possible interpretation is that increased permanence in the center when the child is present reflected an overall reduction in movement (i.e., more "freezing") in that condition, contrary to rodent findings 1 . To test this possibility, we next assessed freezing-like behavior in parents, using physiological and kinematic parameters.

Heart rate, in particular heart rate deceleration or bradycardia, has been frequently used as a proxy for freezing in humans 25 . To further determine whether the presence of children was associated with changes in freezing-related behavior, we analyzed parents' heart rate, recorded via pulse plethysmography. Specifically, we modelled average heart rate (in beats-per-minute) as a function of condition and phase. A significant effect of condition was observed (β(withchild)=1.57, SE=0.66, t=2.38, p=0.020; Table S21), with higher heart rate recorded, across phases, when the child was present. Additionally, we found heart rate varied significantly as a function of phase (β(post-encounter)=-3.30, SE=0.37, t=-8.87, p<0.001; β(circa-strike)=5.13, SE=0.45, t=11.31, p<0.001, Figure 2c), with higher heart rate during circa-strike relative to preand post-encounter and during pre-relative to post-encounter. That slowest heart rate was recorded during post-encounter is consistent with the predatory imminence framework, which points to freezing as a first-line defensive strategy in mammals when a threat is first detected 26.

When pooling together data from both samples, significant heart rate variation as a function of phase remained, but there were no significant effect or interactions involving condition or sample (Table S28), suggesting that higher heart rate in the presence of a child might not depend on kinship. Nonetheless, when the unrelated-child sample was tested separately, heart rate varied based on phase akin to the own-child sample (β(post-encounter)=-2.92, SE=0.59, t=-4.91, p<0.001; β(circa-strike)=4.12, SE=0.85, t=4.87, p<0.001), but not as a function child presence (β(with-child)=-0.03, SE=1.00, t=-0.03, p=0.978; Figure 2c).

In addition to heart rate, kinematic parameters were examined. Specifically, we tested whether the maximum distance covered by the parent relative to their starting position varied as a function of condition and phase. We found no evidence that distance from starting position varied based on the presence of children (β(with-child)=-0.001, SE=0.02, t=-0.05, p=0.956). In terms of phase, shortest distance was covered during post-encounter (β(post-encounter)=-0.20, SE=0.01, t=-19.04, p<0.001), and largest in circa-strike; β(circa-strike)=0.41, SE=0.02, t=22.31, p<0.001; Table S32), consistent with the fact that during that phase participants could approach the attacker to fight back.

We also modelled the amount of motion and observed a significant increase across all phases, when the own child was present (β(with-child)=0.01, SE=0.004, t=2.01, p=0.048), an effect that was absent in the unrelated-child sample (β(with-child)=0.01, SE=0.01, t=0.99, p=0.331).

Relative to phase, smallest amount of motion was recorded during post-encounter (β(post-encounter)=-0.05, SE=0.002, t=-27.14, p<0.001) and greatest in circa-strike (β(circa-strike)=0.09, SE=0.003, t=28.06, p<0.001; Table S40).

Taken together, our results suggest that increased time spent in the center of the environment did not reflect reduced movement in the presence of one's own child. Rather, our findings are consistent with observations in rodents that parents reduce freezing, reflected here in elevated heart rate and increased head movement, while simultaneously maintaining closer physical proximity to their offspring.

Faster parental active avoidance in the presence of own children

We next examined how parental defensive behaviors directed at the threat varied based on child presence by focusing on epochs when there was an attack (circa-strike). Parents were instructed that they could reduce the probability of receiving a shock by walking towards the attacker and repeatedly pressing a button on the hand-held controller. To quantify parental active defensive behavior during this phase, we modelled movement (peak velocity and peak acceleration), arm positioning and kinematics (arm angle and acceleration), and pressing behavior (number and speed of correct clicks). We found both peak velocity (β(with-child)=0.08, SE=0.03, t=3.17, p=0.002; Figure 2e; Table S48) and peak acceleration to be significantly higher when the child was present (β(with-child)=0.90, SE=0.17, t=5.17, p<0.001; Figure 2f; Table S52). Likewise, arm acceleration was higher as a function of child presence (β(with-child)= 0.003, SE=0.001, t=2.92, p=0.004; Figure 2f; Table S57). Importantly, none of these effects were observed in the presence of an unrelated child (Tables S49, S53 and S58; Figure 2e-g). When modelling both samples together, interactions between condition and sample were found (peak velocity: β(with-child: unrelated-child)=-0.09, SE=0.04, t=-1.97, p=0.051; peak acceleration: β(with-child: unrelatedchild)=-0.66, SE=0.30, t=-2.21, p=0.029; Tables S50 and S53), driven by significant differences between alone and with-child conditions only in the own-child sample (pairwise comparisons, peak velocity: own-child p=0.002; unrelated-child sample p=0.890; peak acceleration: own-child p<0.001; unrelated-child p=0.336; Tables S51 and S56). For arm acceleration, the interaction between condition and sample was not significant (β(with-child: unrelated-child)=-0.002, SE=0.001, t=-1.38, p=0.170; Table S60), however, pairwise comparisons yielded the same pattern as the other measures, with condition differences in the own-child sample only (ownchild p=0.003; unrelated-child p=0.554; Table S61). We found no evidence that child presence influenced parental arm positioning (β(with-child)=-0.10, SE=0.49, t=-0.21, p=0.837; Table S63), pressing responses (correct clicks: β(with-child)=0.12, SE=0.12, z=1.05, p=0.296; correct click speed: β(with-child)=-0.09, SE=0.13, t=-0.70, p=0.488; Table S67 and S71) or time in the correct sensor (β(with-child)=0.03, SE=0.01, t=1.91, p=0.060; Table S81).

Taken together, our results suggest that the presence of one's own child modulates defensive behavior in parents by suppressing freezing and promoting more efficient active avoidance that allows for increased physical proximity to the child. Importantly, this modulation of defensive behavior was directly linked with parental defense, as similar effects were not observed when an unrelated child was present. the center (g). Presence versus absence of children can be predicted from multivariate parental behavior

Leveraging the high dimensionality of our dataset, we also undertook a multivariate approach to determine whether combined behavioral, kinematic and physiological parental indices distinguished between alone and own-child conditions. In other words, this approach allowed us to assess whether the presence/absence of offspring could be predicted based on parental defense as a whole. An elastic-net logistic-regression classifier was trained using all behavioral, kinematic and physiological parameters recorded, per phase, from parents in the own-child sample. Model performance was evaluated through participant-grouped nested cross-validation (30 repetitions). The mean Area Under the Receiving Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC AUC) across the 30 outer cross-validation repetitions was 0.82 (SD=0.02; range=[0.78-0.85]; Table S85), indicating that the classifier reliably discriminated between alone and with-child conditions (Figure 3b). Next, out-of-fold predicted probabilities were averaged across the 30 outer crossvalidation repetitions for each participant-condition observation, yielding an AUC of 0.84 (bootstrap 95% CI=[0.79-0.89]; Figure 3a; Table S86), which exceeded the null distribution generated by permuting condition labels within participants (pperm<0.001; Figure 3c). Overall, these results indicate that the classifier discriminated, above-chance, the presence and absence of a parent's own child based on the defensive pattern expressed.

To determine whether this pattern generalized beyond parent-child interactions, we applied the model developed in the own-child sample to the unrelated-child sample. The model discriminated the alone and with-child conditions above chance, with the observed AUC exceeding the permutation-generated null distribution (pperm<0.001; Figure 3f). However, the AUC was lower than in the own-child sample (0.71; bootstrap 95% CI=[0.60, 0.80]; Figure 3d; Table S91), pointing to partial rather than complete generalization across samples. These results suggest that the presence of a child, regardless of kinship, can be discriminated based on overall defensive pattern, but this discrimination is the most accurate when in the presence of one's own child.

Next, we assessed whether the defensive pattern that discriminated alone and with-child conditions was qualitatively different between the own-and unrelated-child samples. For each participant and feature, a child-presence-related change was calculated as:

ΔX=Xwith-child -Xalone

These participant-level change scores were then entered into an elastic-net classifier predicting whether participants belonged to the own-or unrelated-child sample. A mean ROC AUC of 0.64 (SD=0.03; range=[0.54-0.70]; Table S94) across 30 outer cross-validation repetitions suggested a moderate but better than chance discrimination between the two samples. The AUC calculated from repetition-averaged out-of-fold probabilities was 0.65 (bootstrap 95% CI=[0.54, 0.75]; Figure 3g; Table S95), and exceeded the permutation-generated null distribution (pperm=0.018; Figure 3i). These results suggest that the multivariate defensive pattern that discriminated alone and with-child conditions differed reliably between the own-and unrelated-child samples. generalization of the condition classifier to the unrelated-child sample. d. Observational threat learning in children was stronger from parents than unrelated adults Our second goal was to determine how parental defensive behavior shapes the transmission of threat information between parent and child. Studies in rat dams have shown that freezing suppression in combination with closer proximity to pups during threat exposure is associated with enhanced threat learning by offspring 1 . Accordingly, we hypothesized that parental active defense in humans would facilitate threat learning by their children. To test this hypothesis, we assessed observational threat learning using both physiological and explicit measures. During the with-child condition (acquisition), children's skin conductance responses (SCRs) to the CS+ (sounds preceding attacks on the parent) and CS-(sounds never preceding attacks) were recorded. Following the task, children were tested alone in the VR environment, where the same sounds were replayed while SCRs were recorded and participants rated how likely each sound was to be followed by an attack on the parent (attack expectancy). Indicators of child threat learning were modelled in a series of linear mixed models using parental behavior, CS type (CS + or CS-) and trial number as predictors. If parental defensive behavior meaningfully impacts observational threat learning in children, we would expect significant interactions between CS type and parental behavior, reflecting the influence of parental behavior on the differentiation between CS+ and CS-by the child.

During the acquisition phase, children in the own-child sample showed greater SCRs to CS+ than to CS-(β(CS+)=0.14, SE=0.01, t=8.68, p<0.001; Table S99), with follow-up comparisons confirming that significant CS+/CS-differentiation occurred for all three sounds (all ps<0.001; Table S100). When both samples were modelled together, a CS type by sample interaction indicated weaker differentiation in the unrelated-child sample (β(CS+: unrelated-child)=-0.05, SE=0.02, t=-2.14, p=0.034; Table S102). Follow-up comparisons confirmed significant differentiation in both samples, but stronger in the own-child sample (Table S104). Specifically, differentiation was significant across all three sounds in the own-child sample but only for the final two sounds in the unrelated-child sample (Figure 4a; Table S105).

We found no evidence that parental variables (including parental distance) were reliably associated with children's SCR differentiation between the CS+ and CS-(Tables S107,S109 and S113). Thus, children differentiated threat from safe cues during observation, with stronger differentiation when observing the parent versus an unrelated adult, but this pattern was not reliably explained by specific parental defensive behaviors.

During the subsequent test phase, children showed no significant SCR differentiation between CS+ and CS-(β(CS+)=0.01, SE=0.01, t=0.53, p=0.596; Table S115), and differentiation did not differ between samples (β(CS+: unrelated-child)=-0.003, SE=0.02, t=-0.12, p=0.905; Table S117).

Likewise, explicit attack-expectancy ratings did not significantly differ between CS+ and CS-(β(CS+)=0.01, SE=0.01, t=1.05, p=0.297; Table S126), and no differences were found between samples (β(CS+: unrelated-child)=-0.02, SE=0.15, t=-0.11, p=0.914; Table S128).

Interestingly, we found that parental distance was associated with overall attack expectancy differently across samples. In the own-child sample, higher attack-expectancy was associated with shorter distance from the parent (β(distance)=-0.19, SE=0.08, t=-2.44, p=0.016; Table S136), whereas in the unrelated-child sample it was associated with greater distance from the unrelated adult (Figure 4b). This suggests that the effect depends on the relationship with the adult, and that physical proximity to the parent might enhance the overall salience of threatrelevant information in children.

Taken together, our results showed that children physiologically differentiated cues predicting an attack on the adult, with stronger observational learning from the parent than from an unrelated adult. Also, greater proximity to the parent during threat exposure was associated with later higher attack expectancy for both safety and threat cues. This suggests that physical closeness to the parent in a dangerous situation may enhance the overall salience of contextrelevant information in children. to each stimulus. Attack expectancy ratings as a function of mean parental distance from the child for the own-child and unrelated-child groups. Lines show model-predicted slopes from with 95% confidence bands; points show observed mean ratings ± standard errors within tertiles of distance. **p < 0.01.

Multivariate parental behavior did not predict children's threat learning

We next asked whether the multivariate pattern of parental behavioral, kinematic and physiological responses predicted subsequent threat learning in children. Four elastic-net regression models were fitted to predict complementary indices of differential threat learning: the CS+ versus CS-skin-conductance response (SCR) to the second sound during the task (acquisition); the CS+ versus CS-skin conductance difference after the task (test; first three trials per CS); the CS+ versus CS-difference in post-task attack-expectancy ratings; and a composite learning score defined as the first principal component of differential SCRs to all three sounds during acquisition and test together with differential attack-expectancy ratings. None of the four models provided evidence for a multivariate parental defensive signature enhancing threat learning in children (see Supplementary Information).

Discussion

Our findings identify offspring presence as a key determinant of human defensive strategy selection. Consistent with animal models, offspring presence shifted defensive responses away from passive states and toward active forms of offspring protection. This reorganization was evident across behavioral, physiological, and kinematic measures, which taken together revealed a coordinated defensive state characterized by increased offspring proximity, reduced freezing-related responses, and enhanced active avoidance. Importantly, these effects were absent, attenuated or qualitatively different in the presence of unrelated children, suggesting that they cannot be solely explained by a general social-presence effect.

Regardless of threat imminence (i.e., across pre-encounter, post-encounter and circa-strike phases), parents prioritized physical closeness to their child. These findings resonate with rodent work showing that, under threat, female rats accompanied by older pups (19 to 21 days postpartum) predominantly display pup-directed behaviors, including keeping close contact with them, nursing and grooming them 1 . These behaviors replaced freezing, the dominant behavioral response otherwise expressed if the animal was alone. Similarly, we show that greater proximity to the child was complemented by a reduction in freezing-related bradycardia and increased movement in parents accompanied by their child. This striking parallel between human and rodent findings relies on the assumption that heart rate, in particular heart rate deceleration, is a proxy for human freezing 25 . Our results supported this by showing that, across samples, heart rate reliably decreased with initial threat detection (post-encounter) and subsequently increased, reaching maximum values during active avoidance (circa-strike). This pattern of heart rate variation as a function of threat imminence is consistent with theoretical predictions regarding the role of freezing in threat evaluation and response preparation along the defensive continuum 25 , validating the use of heart rate as a robust indicator of human freezing in our task.

Our results also showed differences in active avoidance by parents when their child was present relative to alone. Specifically, during imminent threat (circa-strike) parents displayed more vigorous active defensive behavior, namely by moving faster and spending more time fighting off the attacker. When taken together with our effects on spatial proximity to the child and freezing reduction, the intensification of active avoidance suggests that offspring presence may enhance the precision of defensive behavior in parents: in order to both maintain closeness to the child and avoid the threat, active avoidance becomes more targeted and efficient. This is consistent with the idea that human parental defense reflects a coordinated strategy that optimizes both offspring access and threat avoidance.

Our results are partially aligned with previous evidence 27 and theoretical accounts 28 suggesting that parenthood in humans reorganizes threat perception in order to maximize caregiving, including by boosting attentional processes in the presence of infantile cues. However, these accounts emphasize the generalization of defensive adaptations to care for infants regardless of kinship, largely due to humans being a alloparental species that is acutely attuned to infantile cues 28, 29 . The comparison between these accounts and our study is limited by the fact that we tested older children, presumably perceived as less vulnerable than infants. Nonetheless, our results showed that key defensive behavioral adaptations (namely, prioritization of closeness to child, freezing reduction and increased avoidance precision) manifested specifically in the presence of own children, not generalizing to the presence of an age-matched non-related child.

When considering the multivariate pattern of parental defense, spanning movement, physiology, action execution and spatial positioning indicators, results showed partial generalization to unrelated dyads, although the classification accuracy was highest in the presence of one's own child. This suggests that overall parental defense may comprise general social components but is highly kin-specific.

Our findings converge with previous reports in rodent models, suggesting that the adaptive functions of parental defense are conserved across mammals even when their behavioral manifestations differ between species 30, 31 . This convergence raises the possibility that the neural mechanisms underlying parental protection are also shared between humans and other mammals. At the neurohormonal level, maternal care and defense in lactating animals are promoted by neuropeptides oxytocin, vasopressin, and prolactin, in combination with downregulation of the corticotropin-releasing factor system 32 . Oxytocin release in the central amygdala is likely to play an especially important role in parental defense beyond the postpartum stage, since it is implicated in switching between freezing and active avoidance both during selfdefense 33 and pup protection 1 . This is consistent with the idea that self-and other-protection rely on shared defensive neural circuitry 34 . The presumed neural mechanisms underlining our effects remain, however, speculative in the absence of direct neural measures.

One notable difference between our study and research in rodents is that studies in rodents are primarily conducted in females given sex exclusivity in caregiving roles. This is presumably why female rodents display overall varying defensive strategies from males, even in the absence of offspring (for instance, predominance of "darting" over freezing 35, 36 ), reflecting a built-in tendency to express defensive strategies adaptive not only for self-defense but also for pup protection 8 . Although our study included both males and females, about 81% of our sample was composed of mothers, raising the possibility that the reported effects primarily reflect 20 evolutionarily conserved maternal protection strategies in mammals. Additional research with balanced numbers of mothers and fathers is warranted to test this possibility.

The second goal of our study was to examine the transmission of threat information in parentchild dyads. Results provided evidence of observational threat learning in children: during threat exposure in the presence of the parent, skin conductance response was enhanced to the CS+ relative to the CS-. These effects were attenuated in children accompanied by an unrelated adult, matching previous demonstrations of stronger vicarious learning from parents relative to strangers 21 , and standing at odds with reports of comparable observational learning from both 22, 37 . One possibility is that the greater naturalism and complexity of our VR paradigm amplified the relative importance of the parent as a source of threat information. In simpler observational learning paradigms, the task demands may be sufficiently low for children to acquire threat associations from both parents and unfamiliar adults. Parents may represent a particularly potent channel for the transmission of threat information in more complex environments. Consistent with this interpretation, studies in rodents demonstrate that offspring acquire threat-related information directly from maternal defensive responses, via amygdaladependent social transmission mechanisms 38, 39.

In addition to differential task demands, the current paradigm also differed from traditional observational-learning tasks in that parental behavior was less experimentally constrained. This allowed us to assess how specific features of parental defense affected the transmission of threat information to children. We found that, regardless of whether initial learning occurred in the presence of the parent or an unrelated adult, attack expectancy afterwards did not differ for cues of threat (CS+) and safety (CS-). However, closer proximity to the parent during initial exposure led to subsequent overall enhancement of attack expectation in children. This effect was only found in children that had been exposed to threat in the present of their parent (and not an unrelated adult), and generalized to both threat and safe cues (CS+ and CS-). These results are not entirely consistent with rodent findings, which showed that proximity to the progenitor during threat exposure predicted subsequent conditioned freezing 1 . Our findings suggest that, rather that improving the discrimination of threat and safety, parental proximity may enhance the overall salience of information presented in a dangerous context. One possible mechanism accounting for this effect is attentional: physical proximity may increase children's attention to both parental behavior and context, making all cues more salient and easily encoded. Future work directly manipulating physical proximity between parent and child would allow for the examination of a potential causal role in the social transmission of threat.

Some limitations of our study should be considered. One is that, despite the increased naturalism of our paradigm relative to other experimental approaches, threats still occurred in a virtual environment and did not present genuine danger. Despite this, our findings were largely consistent with research in rodents that uses potent threats, strengthening our interpretations.

Another relevant aspect is that in our paradigm only the parent was under threat. Although motivated by ethical concerns, this methodological decision limits the interpretation that defensive changes in parents when the child was present are related to offspring protection.

Systematically varying whether only the parent, the child or both are under threat would more precisely inform about how parental behavioral is recalibrated to promote offspring survival specifically. Nonetheless, that our findings were consistent with rodent studies, and that several effects were not found in unrelated-dyads, supports that defensive changes in parents likely reflect behavioral adaptations for offspring protection. Practical limitations should also be acknowledged. For instance, the size of the testing room may have also constrained the variability of kinematics measures, limiting our ability to detect subtle effects. Room size also precluded the possibility of varying the child's position, which would have allowed us to experimentally dissociate the distance from the center of the environment from the distance to the child. Finally, the age range of the children was limited and, for ethical reasons, only older children were included. This prevented us from determining the impact of child age on parental defensive behavior.

Conclusions

Parental care is typically conceptualized as being supported by systems specialized for caregiving, attachment, and nurturance. Our findings suggest that it is also supported by defensive adaptations that reshape how humans respond to danger. Similar to other mammals, offspring presence induced a distinct functional defensive pattern in human parents, characterized by increased proximity to offspring, inhibition of freezing and more efficient active avoidance. Further, our findings highlighted how parental defensive behavior may contribute not only to protection of offspring but also to the intergenerational transmission of threat information. In sum, the present study supports a reconceptualization of parental defense as an evolutionarily conserved, coordinated behavioral state that serves both protective and developmental functions.

Materials and methods

Participants

Sample size was decided based on power calculations and availability of resources. It was estimated that, to detect a medium effect size (d=0.30) on a within-subject comparison with two conditions at α=0.05 with 80% power, a sample of 90 dyads would be necessary. Additionally, to detect a moderate correlation (r=0.3; e.g., between child SCR and parental defensive behavior), a sample of 84 dyads would be required. Taking these estimates into account together with resource availability, a sample of 85 parent-child dyads was collected for the main experiment (own-child sample). One dyad was excluded due to a technical issue with the VR task, which left us with a sample of 84 parent-child dyads. Both (biological) mothers and fathers were included (n(mothers)=68; n(fathers)=16). Children were between 13 and 16 years of age. Age range for the children was decided based on the nature of the experimental task and stimuli, which could be frightening or distressing to younger children. Recruitment was conducted through flyers, social media advertisements, and outreach via school administrations and parent networks in the Stockholm area.

To assess whether any observed effects generalized to non-kin dyads, an independent sample of parent-unrelated child dyads was additionally recruited (add age/sex breakdown). The required sample size for the unrelated-child experiment was decided by conducting a post hoc power simulation 40 to evaluate the sensitivity of the own-child sample to detect the observed effect of condition on the average distance from the center of the environment in the own-child sample.

The simulation was based on the linear mixed-effects model used in the analysis, with average distance from center as the dependent variable, condition as a fixed effect, and a maximal random structure including a random intercept and random slope for condition by participant.

One thousand datasets were generated for each sample size using the parameter estimates obtained from the fitted model: β0=0.53, βcondition= -0.053, σ0=0.112 (random intercept standard deviation), σcondition=0.115 (random slope standard deviation), a correlation of -0.14 between the random intercept and slope, and a residual standard deviation of 0.118. Each simulated dataset reproduced the same structure as the empirical data, including the number of observations per participant. For each simulated dataset, the same linear mixed-effects model was fitted and statistical significance for the coefficient of interest (the fixed effect of condition) was assessed with α=0.05. Power for each sample size was defined as the proportion of simulated datasets in which the condition effect was detected as significant. This method suggested that 44 participants would be required to achieve 80% power for the effect of interest. Due to practical constraints on recruitment and data collection, 40 participants were enrolled. After exclusion of two participants for technical reasons, the final analyzed unrelated-child sample consisted of 38 participants. Under the same simulation framework, such a sample size corresponded to an estimated power of approximately 70%, indicating reduced sensitivity relative to conventional 80% targets. This sample therefore provided somewhat lower sensitivity than the nominal target, and results should be interpreted accordingly.

For both the own-and unrelated-child samples, exclusion criteria included intellectual disabilities, history of relevant neurological or psychiatric disorders, ongoing medication known to affect autonomic responding (e.g., benzodiazepines and beta-blockers), and significant visual, auditory or motor impairments that limited performance of the experimental tasks.

Participation took place in one session at the Karolinska Institute (Stockholm, Sweden). Data for the own-child sample was collected between April and October 2025, while data for the unrelated-child sample was collected between January and March 2026. Detailed information about both samples demographics is provided in Table S1. Adult participants provided informed consent prior to participation, and children provided assent. Participants were compensated for their participation, and the study was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Etikprövningsmyndigheten).

Experimental tasks

Parents Parents (N=85) performed a defense task in a Virtual Reality (VR) environment, in which they were required to respond to a virtual attacker. The virtual environment depicted a forest at night; participants were asked to imagine that they had gone camping and that, while in their tent, heard a noise and realized there was an attacker outside. Task design was inspired by the predatory imminence continuum 19 , and each trial included three phases: in the pre-encounter phase (12-20 s), no attacker was visible in the environment; in the post-encounter phase (10-18 s), the attacker could be seen walking in the distance at one of three walking speeds (slow: 16 s, medium: 12 s, or fast: 10 s); finally, during circa-strike (15 s), the attacker would run towards the participant wielding a saw (Figure 1A). The attack could occur from three possible directionsfront, left and right (Figure 1B). To maximize naturalism of the task and capture a range of spontaneous defensive behaviors, it was emphasized to participants that different behaviors were possible in the task, including retreating back towards the tent, staying immobile, or approaching the attacker. Importantly, it was stressed that the most adaptive behavior at each point depended on the context and behavior of the attacker. That is, if the attacker was far, limited movement could prevent detection (and subsequent attack); conversely, if an attack was ongoing, there was the possibility of fighting back. To do so, participants should move towards the attacker and repeatedly press a button on a handheld controlled (which in the virtual environment was visualized as hitting the attacker with a stick). Participants were informed that fighting back would decrease the probability that the attack would result in an aversive electrical shock to the wrist. Half the trials were attack trials. Of these, 50% were shock trials. On shock trials, fighting back successfully reduced the probability of receiving a shock from 100% to 50% (the exact shock contingencies were not communicated to participants). On no-attack trials (7 s), after post-encounter, the attacker would run back rather than initiating an attack.

Participants performed the task in two blocks, corresponding to two conditions with counterbalanced order: alone and with-child. In the with-child condition, instructions were identical, with the exception that participants were asked to imagine that they had gone camping with their daughter/son. The dyad shared the same VR environment, such that the participant could see an avatar of the child standing next to the tent, and the child could see an avatar of the parent performing the task (Figure 1a). The child had a passive role in the task: they were not required to perform any responses, and were not under threat of shock. Each block comprised 18 trials (9 attack and 9 no-attack). The order of attack and no-attack trials, and attack directions (front, left, right) were pseudo-randomized within blocks.

For the control experiment (N=40), an identical task was used. Here, participants performed the task alone and with the unrelated child, in counterbalanced order.

Children

Children (N=84) performed two tasks in the VR environment in sequential order: acquisition and test. The Acquisition corresponded to the parent's with-child condition. It entailed an observational learning procedure wherein children learned to associate an environmental auditory cue (conditioned stimulus, CS+) with the occurrence of an attack on the parent (unconditioned stimulus, US). To maintain naturalism, auditory cues were the sound of either an owl or a frog, Source recordings were selected from Pixabay (copyright-free media) and trimmed to 1.2 s segments containing a single vocalization. The two clips were chosen to have waveform envelopes that were as similar as possible. Background noise was reduced using a spectralgating denoising procedure implemented with the reduce_noise function from the Python noisereduce module, removing incidental sounds present in the original recordings. To equate signal intensity, the owl clip was then linearly amplified to match the peak amplitude of the frog clip. Assignment of the two sounds to CS+ and CS-was counterbalanced across participants.

The CS+ or CS-role for each cue was counterbalanced across participants.

the distant phalanx of participant's non-dominant indicator finger. For children, two electrodes were placed on the distal phalanges of the non-dominant indicator and middle fingers, for recording of skin conductance responses. Physiological signal was sampled at 1000 Hz.

Procedure

Upon arrival, all participants received a brief introduction to the VR laboratory, were provided with written study information, and gave written informed consent before the experiment began. In the unrelated-child sample, the adult and child were introduced to one another and exchanged names prior to reading the study information and providing consent. Before being welcomed into the experimental room, all unrelated participants were assigned to separate waiting areas, where they were not permitted to communicate or interact until the experimental session began. Throughout the experimental session, communication between the adult and child was kept to a minimum, as participants primarily listened to instructions (Supplementary information) and informational presentations delivered by the experimenter. During the experiment, inside VR, verbal communication was not permitted, and any interaction was limited to non-verbal communication.

Shock calibration, VR setup and physiological baseline

Following electrode placement, participants underwent an individualized shock calibration procedure to determine a stimulation intensity perceived as "very uncomfortable" but not painful. Calibration started at 15 V and increased incrementally. After each stimulation, participants rated the perceived intensity on a 9-point subjective discomfort scale (1=not uncomfortable at all;9=very uncomfortable). Participants were instructed to aim for a rating of 9, with the understanding that a rating of 9 represented "very uncomfortable" rather than pain.

After calibration, both members of the dyad were equipped with the VR equipment and placed in the virtual environment. A one-minute physiological baseline recording was collected before the experimental procedure. Before the experimental trials, participants were familiarized with the virtual environment and their avatars. When both parent and child were present in the VR environment, they were instructed to verify each other's avatar identity by waving at each other.

Child-only test phase

During the child-only test phase, children entered the same virtual environment without their parent. Before entering the virtual environment, they were informed that they would hear the same sounds encountered earlier in the experiment and that, after hearing each sound several times, they would answer two questions regarding (1) how much they would expect an attack when hearing that sound while accompanied by their parent, and (2) how threatening they perceived the sound to be. In line with previous research, expectancy ratings were used in the analysis as an indicator of observational threat learning in the child 42 . Responses were provided using 5-point Likert scales, ranging from 1 ("low expectation") to 5 ("high expectation") for expected attack probability (threat ratings were not analyzed for hypothesis testing).

Following the experiment, both parent and child completed a series of questionnaires assessing demographics, post-task ratings, and personality traits (full description in Supplementary Information).

Data preprocessing

SCR preprocessing

Skin conductance responses (SCRs) were recorded continuously from the child throughout the experiment and the raw signal was subsequently preprocessed offline. The skin conductance signal was band-pass filtered between 0.05 and 1 Hz to reduce slow signal drift and highfrequency noise.

Conditioned SCR magnitude was extracted separately for each conditioned stimulus (CS) trial.

Responses were quantified as the maximum peak-to-peak amplitude change in skin conductance (µS) occurring within a 0.5-4.5 s response window following stimulus onset. Trials in which the peak-to-peak response amplitude was below 0.02 µS were considered nonresponses and assigned a value of zero.

Following response extraction, SCR values were square-rooted to address skewness prior to statistical analyses.

PPG preprocessing

Photoplethysmography (PPG) signal collected from the parent was band-pass filtered between 0.5 and 8 Hz using a second-order Butterworth filter and smoothed using a third-order Savitzky-Golay filter with an approximately 80 ms window. Systolic peaks were initially identified separately within each epoch using a custom derivativebased algorithm. The positive first derivative of the PPG signal was squared and smoothed over approximately 150 ms. Candidate pulse upstrokes were identified using an adaptive threshold defined as the rolling median plus 0.5 times the median absolute deviation within a 3 s window.

The maximum signal amplitude occurring within 300 ms of each candidate onset was retained as the pulse peak. Potential duplicate detections occurring within 250 ms were merged, and a minimum interpeak interval of 350 ms was imposed.

Interbeat intervals were screened using physiological limits of 300-1500 ms, corresponding to pulse rates of 40-200 beats per minute. Intervals were additionally flagged when they or their successive changes deviated by more than 25% from the local median calculated across an 11beat window. Intervals greater than 1.8 times or smaller than 0.6 times the local median were flagged as potential missed or additional beats, respectively. These automated flags were used to support quality control. All epochs were subsequently visually inspected. Incorrectly detected peaks were manually corrected, and signal intervals containing unrecoverable noise were excluded from following analyses. Epochs containing fewer than two corrected peaks or no valid interbeat intervals were assigned missing heart-rate values.

Instantaneous heart rate was calculated as 60,000 divided by the interbeat interval in milliseconds. Mean, minimum and maximum heart rates were computed from the valid intervals in each phase. Resulting by-phase average heart rate values greater than 220 beats per minute were considered artifacts and therefore treated as missing in following analyses.

Movement tracking and feature extraction

Head-position data were obtained from the head-mounted display, whereas arm position was recorded using an additional tracker positioned above the elbow. Both signals were sampled at 10 Hz.

Arm-position coordinates were first expressed relative to the participant's head by subtracting the concurrent head position from the three-dimensional arm-tracker position. Arm-tracker artifacts were identified from the resulting relative trajectory using thresholds of 2 m/s for threedimensional speed and 20 m/s² for acceleration magnitude. Samples immediately preceding and following each detected artifact were also flagged. Internal gaps lasting no more than 0.5 s were reconstructed using linear interpolation. If more than 30% of a phase was flagged, the trajectory was not reconstructed. Trajectories without remaining missing samples were subsequently smoothed using a second-order Savitzky-Golay filter with a 0.5s window. All epochs were subsequently visually inspected to ensure signal quality.

Head movement was quantified in the horizontal plane from the x-and z-coordinates, whereas relative arm movement was quantified in three dimensions. Samplewise displacement was calculated as the Euclidean distance between consecutive samples. Total movement was defined as the sum of these samplewise distances within each phase. For head movement, the minimum, maximum and mean distances from the centre of the virtual environment were calculated, together with the maximum and mean distances from the participant's position at phase onset and the variance of distance from that starting position. For arm movement, the maximum and mean distances from the arm position at phase onset and the variance of this distance were calculated. Instantaneous speed was calculated by dividing samplewise displacement by the 100 ms sampling interval. Acceleration was calculated as the change in speed between consecutive samples divided by the sampling interval. The minimum, maximum and mean speed and acceleration were retained separately for head and arm movement. Because acceleration was calculated from changes in scalar speed, negative values reflected deceleration.

A relative arm-angle measure was calculated from the head-corrected arm-tracker coordinates with respect to the downward vertical axis, such that 0° indicated a downward-pointing vector, 90° a horizontal vector and 180° an upward-pointing vector. The mean, minimum, maximum and variance of this angle were calculated within each phase. The corresponding summaries were also calculated for the absolute change in angle from its value at phase onset.

Movement features were first calculated separately for each trial and phase. For the multivariate analyses, valid trial-level estimates were averaged within participant, experimental condition and task phase. Arm-derived variables were coded as missing for 4 participants with unusable arm-tracker recordings; subsequent imputation and standardization were performed within the relevant cross-validation training sets.

Detailed information about kineamtic features processing and analysis is provided in Supplementary Information.

Behavioral actions and sensor-use features

Behavioral events were extracted for each trial and task phase. The virtual environment contained five prespecified regions of interest: front, left, right and tent regions, and the center of the environment. These regions consisted of squared "sensors" with sides of 0.75 meters surrounding the center of the environment and centered at (0,0.50), (0.75,-0.25), (-0.75,-0.25), (0,-1.25) and (0,0) m, respectively. For each trial and phase, the latency to first entry and total time spent in each region were calculated. Time spent in the central area, outside all predefined regions and outside the three response-sensor regions was also calculated from the head spatial coordinates. For every recorded visit to one of these regions, we extracted the latency from phase onset to region entry, the duration of the stay, the latency to exit, the number of controller clicks and a click-speed measure. Region-specific variables additionally quantified the number of entries and the total and mean dwell duration for each region.

Click-related features included the total number of clicks produced during each phase and the numbers produced in one of the attack-related sensors or outside these predefined regions.

Because participants could produce clicks in one continuous sequence or in multiple temporally separated bursts, click-speed features were summarized across the click-speed values recorded for each burst. These comprised the speed of the first and last click bursts and the minimum, maximum and mean click speed across bursts within the phase.

During the circa-strike phase, the response region located in the direction of the attack was defined as the correct region, whereas the remaining response regions were defined as incorrect regions. Separate features quantified the number of clicks, mean click speed, total dwell duration and latency to first entry for the correct and incorrect regions. Clicks produced outside the response regions were retained separately.

Statistical analysis

All analyses were implemented in R, via lme4 43 and lmerTest 44 and custom-made scripts. The significance threshold was set at α=0.05. The study was preregistered on Open Science Framework, OSF; osf.io/vjrza), but not all analyses described in the paper were included in the initial preregistration. All data and code are available on All data and code are available on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23954350.

Univariate (hypothesis-driven) approach

Parents

To quantify parental defensive behavior during the task, several behavioral measures were recorded (see Data preprocessing above, and Supplementary information for a full list of indices). Among these measures, priority was given to those that indexed theoretically-relevant features of the defensive response. Specifically, to assess the main target of parental defense (whether responses were mainly threat-or child-directed), we used the average distance to the center, and time spent in the center of the environment. To operationalize passive avoidance (freezing), we used the maximum distance from starting position (i.e., distance covered by the parent relative to their starting position at the beginning of each phase), total head motion and heart rate. Finally, to operationalize active avoidance, we focused on indices related to movement speed (peak velocity and acceleration), arm positioning (arm angle and acceleration) pressing behavior (number and speed of correct button presses on the controller) and time spent in the correct sensor (sensor where an attack was ongoing) during circa-strike. Data analysis was conducted with Linear Mixed Models (LMMs), which allow for explicit modelling of the outcome variance explained by participant sampling (random effects), in addition to the main effects of interest (fixed effects). For each identified parental variable, LMMs were used to predict outcome measures as a function of fixed effects phase (pre-encounter, post-encounter and circa-strike) and condition (alone, with-child). For number of clicks, a Generalized LMM with a Poisson likelihood was used to account for the count nature of the variable. For fixed-effects, contrasts for categorical variables were sum-coded,, whereas continuous predictors were standardized using the grand mean and standard deviation (zscored). The sample variable was treatment-coded (own-child = 0, unrelated-child = 0) to facilitate interpretation of the fixed-effect estimates relative to the own-child group. Model assumptions (normality and homoskedasticity of residuals, and normality of random effects residuals), and multicollinearity were checked for all models. Random intercepts and slopes were included by default in all models, and sequentially dropped (based on amount of random variance explained) if the models failed to converge. Analyses focused initially on establishing the effects on the own-child sample only, in line with the pre-registration, and given that the unrelated-child sample was added after the own-child sample data collection was complete. To assess whether observed effects in the own-child sample generalized to the unrelated-child sample, data from both samples were modelled together with an additional fixed effect for sample (own-child, unrelated-child) and all possible interactions. In instances where the inclusion of the interaction term would lead to excessive model complexity (resulting in convergence problems and/or high-order interactions of limited interpretability), we also ran separate models on the unrelated-child sample, focused on assessing the significance of the condition fixed effect.

Children

One of our hypotheses was that observational threat learning by children was associated with parental defensive behavior. To quantify threat learning, we used both physiological and behavioral indices. Specifically, we analyzed the differential skin conductance response of the child to the CS+ and CS-during acquisition, and the subjective ratings attack expectancy provided by the child in the test phase. During acquisition, the first trial was excluded from the analysis, since no learning could occur without at least one pairing of the sound (CS+) with the attack (US). For each of these measures, we used LMMs to estimate the unique contribution of parental defensive behavior measures to child threat learning. We focused specifically on parental behaviors for which significant effects of condition had been identified in the parentfocused analysis. To determine whether learning-related effects generalized across parent-child and adult-unrelated child dyads, we included and interaction with the sample (own-child, unrelated-child) in the modelling. Analogous to the parent-focused analysis, if this resulting in impractical model complexity, separate models on the unrelated-child sample were estimated instead.

Multivariate (data-driven) analyses

We used elastic-net penalized logistic regression to test whether multivariate behavioral, kinematic and physiological (heart rate) profiles discriminated between the with-child and alone conditions. This approach evaluates whether a combination of features distinguishes the two conditions, rather than testing each feature in isolation. Specifically, elastic-net regularization combines ridge and lasso penalties, allowing correlated predictors to be retained while controlling model complexity 45 . The analysis included 147 phase-specific predictors from 84 participants, with each participant contributing one observation per condition; the complete predictor set is reported in Supplementary Tables S88 and S97).

Generalization performance was evaluated using repeated nested participant-grouped crossvalidation 46, 47 . Cross-validation evaluates how well a model predicts observations that were not used to fit it, providing an estimate of its ability to generalize beyond the training data. The outer loop consisted of 10-fold cross-validation repeated 30 times, while model hyperparameters were selected within each outer-training set using repeated five-fold inner cross-validation. This nested procedure separates model selection from performance evaluation, reducing the risk of obtaining overly optimistic estimates when tuning model complexity. Observations belonging to the same participant were assigned to the same fold to prevent information from one participant's observations leaking into both training and test sets . All preprocessing and hyperparameter selection were performed exclusively on training data. Classification performance was quantified using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC AUC), which measures how well the model ranks observations from the two conditions across possible classification thresholds. An AUC of 0.5 indicates chancelevel discrimination, whereas an AUC of 1 indicates perfect discrimination. The primary performance estimate was the mean AUC across the 30 outer cross-validation repetitions. Statistical significance was evaluated using 1,000 within-participant label permutations, with the complete nested cross-validation procedure repeated for each permutation. This test evaluates whether the observed discrimination exceeds what would be expected if condition labels were unrelated to the measured profiles, while preserving the paired structure of the data. Confidence intervals were estimated using participant-level bootstrap resampling to quantify uncertainty in the performance estimate. Full details of preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning, resampling, and permutation testing are provided in Supplementary Information.

To assess cross-sample generalization, a model was developed exclusively in the own-child sample and then applied, without retraining or recalibration, to the independent unrelated-child sample. This analysis tested whether the multivariate pattern associated with child presence generalized to a different sample, rather than reflecting characteristics specific to the participants used to develop the model. Statistical significance of external discrimination was evaluated by permuting condition labels within participants in the independent sample while keeping model predictions fixed.

A second elastic-net logistic-regression analysis tested whether the multivariate response to child presence differed between the own-child and unrelated-child samples. For each predictor, a child-presence change score was calculated as

ΔX=Xwith-child -Xalone

This difference score isolates the within-participant change associated with child presence, reducing the influence of stable between-participant differences in baseline behavior. The resulting 147 change-score predictors were available for 122 participants (84 own-child and 38 unrelated-child). Models were evaluated using the same nested cross-validation framework described above, with folds stratified by sample to preserve sample representation across folds.

Performance was quantified using ROC AUC, and statistical significance was evaluated using permutation testing.

Finally, elastic-net penalized linear regression was used to test whether multivariate behavioral and kinematic profiles predicted individual differences in child threat learning. Four complementary outcomes were considered: the CS+ versus CS-skin-conductance response (SCR) to the second sound during acquisition; the CS+ versus CS-SCR during the test phase, calculated over the first three trials per CS; the CS+ versus CS-difference in post-task attackexpectancy ratings; and a composite learning score defined as the first principal component of differential SCRs during acquisition and test together with differential attack-expectancy ratings. These outcomes captured complementary indicators of threat learning, including physiological discrimination during learning and subsequent testing, explicit expectations of attack, and their shared variance in a composite measure. Using multiple outcomes allowed us to examine whether behavioral and kinematic profiles predicted different aspects of learning rather than relying on a single operationalization. Models were evaluated using the same nested crossvalidation framework, with hyperparameters selected by minimizing root mean squared error (RMSE) in the inner loop. Predictive performance on held-out observations was quantified using RMSE and R² . RMSE measures the typical magnitude of prediction errors in the outcome's units,

Children entered the same VR environment as the parent, and asked to remain still while watching the parent's avatar perform the task. The nine attack trials constituted CS+ trials, for which the CS+ sound was played at three time points, with 0-1 s jittering to reduce the predictability of sound onset: first, in the beginning of the post-encounter phase; second, immediately before the start of the attack (circa-strike); and third, in the middle of an ongoing attack (Figure 1b). CS-sounds were played in no-attack trials at the same time points relative to the start of the trial. Delivering the CS+/-three times (rather than once, as in conventional Pavlovian/observational learning procedures) was meant to facilitate learning in an immersive VR environment, in which the high cognitive load could prevent the sounds from being detected. Indeed, initial piloting suggested that, when playing the sound cues only once, they were easily missed by participants.

During the test phase, children were alone in the same VR environment, but no attacker or parent was present. The CS+ and CS-sounds were presented five times each in randomized order, with each presentation consisting of three consecutive repetitions of the same sound. After each presentation, children were asked to provide two ratings on a 5-point scale: how likely it was that, in the previous block, the sound was associated with an attack on the parent, and how safe they felt after each sound. Main analysis were performed on the attack expectancy ratings, which, in line with prior work 41 , were deemed a more direct measure of contingency learning. Analysis of the safety ratings are available in the Supplementary information.

In the unrelated-child sample, children (N=38) performed identical tasks, with the exception that during acquisition they shared the VR environment with an unrelated adult participant.

Additional information regarding the procedures, as well as a detailed account of self-report measures collected, is available in the Supplementary Information.

Apparatus

The virtual environment and task were programmed on Vizard 7 (Worldviz) and displayed via HTC Vive headsets. Movement in the VR environment was tracked through VR system sensors and ceiling-mounted motion cameras at a sampling frequency of 10 Hz. Electrical shock administration and recording of physiological measures were conducted with a BIOPAC MP150 System and AcqKnowledge 5.0 software. Shocks consisted of 100 ms DC-pulses delivered through two electrodes placed on the adult participants' dominant wrist. Shock intensity was individually calibrated through a work-up procedure, and participants were encouraged to select an intensity that was experienced as "not painful, but very uncomfortable". Additionally, one sensor for recording peripheral blood volume changes (photoplethysmography) was placed on whereas R² quantifies the proportion of outcome variance accounted for by predictions relative to a mean-based reference. Further implementation details are provided in Supplementary Methods.
